questions.q: Imran watches a football roll across the school ground after his friend kicks it. He says, 'The kick put a force into the ball, and the ball carries that force with it as it rolls.' Which statement matches what the chapter says about force?
questions.a: The foot pushes the ball only while they interact; no force travels inside the ball. A force results from the interaction of two objects; when the interaction ceases, neither object experiences that force any more.
o: The foot pushes the ball only while they interact; no force travels inside the ball.
The kick's force stays stored in the ball and is used up little by little as it rolls.
The force on the ball continues after the kick, but the force on the foot stops at once.
A force can belong to the ball alone once the foot has started it moving.

questions.q:
A potter in Khurja presses a lump of wet clay on her wheel with both palms to flatten it.
(a) Name the two objects that interact here, and say whether the force on the clay is a push or a pull.
(b) Does the potter's palm also experience a force? Give the reason the chapter gives.
questions.a: (a) The potter's palms and the clay interact; the force on the clay is a push. (b) Yes. Whenever two objects interact, each object experiences a force from the other, so the clay pushes back on her palms.
s: Names palms and clay as the interacting pair and calls the force a push
Says the palm also feels a force because each interacting object experiences a force from the other

questions.q:
A batter hits a cricket ball. Read three statements.
Statement 1: Only the ball experiences a force; the bat simply gives the force away.
Statement 2: The push of the bat on the ball stops once the ball has left the bat.
Statement 3: If the push measured 40 units of the SI unit of force, it is correctly written as 40 Newton, with a capital N in the word.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only. Statement 1 is wrong because each interacting object experiences a force from the other, so the bat is pushed too. Statement 3 is wrong because the unit is written newton with a small n (symbol N).
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Class 8C of a Visakhapatnam school repeated the box activity with other objects and filled this record.
Row 1: Drawing a bucket of water up a well with a rope | Push | Interacting objects: rope and bucket
Row 2: Pressing a sponge between two palms | Push | Interacting objects: palms and sponge
Row 3: A steel paper clip jumps 2 cm up to a magnet held above it | No force, because nothing touches the clip | Interacting objects: none
Row 4: A cupboard that two boys push equally hard from opposite sides and that does not move | No force acts on the cupboard | Interacting objects: none
(a) Of the two rows that do name a push or a pull, one has named the wrong one. Name that row and correct it.
(b) Correct the whole of Row 3.
(c) Correct Row 4 and explain your correction using what the chapter says about an object that stays at rest.
questions.a: (a) Row 1: drawing the bucket up is a pull (lifting is pulling up), not a push. (b) Row 3: a force does act; it is a pull on the clip, and the magnet and the clip are the interacting objects even though they do not touch. (c) Row 4: forces do act on the cupboard, the push of each boy, so the interacting objects are each boy and the cupboard. An object at rest can have forces acting on it; because the cupboard stays at rest, the forces on it are balancing one another.
s: Picks Row 1 and changes push to pull
Rewrites Row 3 as a pull by the magnet, with magnet and clip as the interacting objects
Says forces from both boys act on the cupboard and that it stays at rest because these forces balance

questions.q: Meena hangs her school bag on a wall hook, and while it hangs the bag pulls the hook down with a force of 30 N. She then lifts the bag clear of the hook and walks away with it. Write the number only: the force, in newton, that the bag now exerts on the hook is ___.
Ayaan moves a heavy crate in four different ways. In which way is the force he applies on the crate the same kind (push or pull) as when he lifts the crate up onto a shelf?
questions.a: Dragging it towards himself by a rope Lifting is pulling up, so the matching action is the other pull: dragging the crate towards himself by the rope. The other three are pushes.
o: Dragging it towards himself by a rope
Shoving it forward with his hands on its back side
Pressing down on its lid to close it firmly
Leaning his back on it to slide it to the wall

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A duster lying still on the teacher's desk has no force acting on it.
Reason (R): If an object stays at rest, the forces acting on it are balancing one another.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. An object at rest can still have forces acting on it; they balance one another, so A is false while R is what the chapter says.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'When Priya pushes hard against the classroom wall and the wall does not move, the wall exerts no force on Priya.'
questions.a: False. Priya's hand and the wall are two interacting objects, and whenever two objects interact, each experiences a force from the other, so the wall pushes on her hand (she can feel it on her palm) even though the wall does not move.
s: States False
Explains that both interacting objects experience a force, so the wall pushes on her hand

questions.q:
Ritu is riding her bicycle slowly across the school ground. Her friend Gopal runs behind her, grips the carrier and holds the bicycle back until it stops. Next time, Gopal stands in front of the bicycle and stops it by pressing on its handlebar with both palms.
(a) Is Gopal's force on the bicycle a push or a pull the first time, and the second time?
(b) Asha says, 'Both times the bicycle stopped, so both forces must be the same kind.' What does the chapter's idea of force tell you about her reasoning?
questions.a: (a) First time: a pull (he holds the bicycle back towards himself from behind). Second time: a push (he presses on the handlebar from the front). (b) Her reasoning is wrong. Whether a force is a push or a pull depends on how it is applied to the object, not on its result; a push and a pull applied from opposite sides can both stop the moving bicycle.
s: Pull from behind the first time, push from the front the second time
Explains that push or pull depends on how the force is applied, not on the effect, so both can stop the bicycle

questions.q:
A teacher hands out five cards. Each card names the object that applies a force. For each card write (i) the object that applies the force, (ii) the object it acts on, and (iii) whether it is a push or a pull. Read each card carefully: some forces are not the obvious one.
Card 1: A boatman in Alappuzha drives his boat forward by pressing his oar back against the water. Give the force the water exerts on the oar.
Card 2: A shopkeeper draws a full water pot up out of a well with a rope. Give the force the rope exerts on the pot.
Card 3: A girl stretches a rubber band between her two thumbs and holds it there. Give the force the rubber band exerts on her right thumb.
Card 4: A pair of bullocks draws a bullock cart along a village road. Give the force the bullocks exert on the cart.
Card 5: A magnet held above a table lifts a steel pin off it. Give the force the magnet exerts on the pin.
questions.a: Card 1: the water applies a push on the oar (the oar pushes the water back and, since both interact, the water pushes the oar forward). Card 2: the rope applies a pull on the pot. Card 3: the stretched rubber band applies a pull on her right thumb (she pulls the band outwards and the band pulls her thumb inwards). Card 4: the bullocks apply a pull on the cart. Card 5: the magnet applies a pull on the pin, without touching it.
s: Card 1: water on oar, push
Card 2: rope on pot, pull
Card 3: rubber band on thumb, pull
Card 4: bullocks on cart, pull
Card 5: magnet on pin, pull without contact

questions.q: A caption under a photo in the science corner reads: 'For a force to act, two objects must interact, and they must be touching each other.' Is the caption right, wrong, or partly right? Support your verdict with one example from the chapter for each half of the caption.
questions.a: Partly right. The caption is right that at least two objects must interact for a force to come into play: when you push a table, the hand and the table interact. It is wrong that they must touch: a magnet exerts a force on another magnet or on a magnetic material without being in contact with it, so interaction does not always mean touching.
s: Gives the verdict partly right
Supports the 'two objects must interact' half with an example such as hand and table
Refutes the 'must touch' half with a non-contact example such as a magnet and a pin

questions.q: A boatman in Srinagar stands in his shikara, presses one end of a long pole against the stone wall of the jetty, and the shikara moves away from the jetty. Which statement about this force is correct?
questions.a: Pole and wall interact, so the wall pushes the pole as the pole pushes it. Whenever two objects interact, each experiences a force from the other; a force can be applied indirectly through a stick, and it is a push here.
o: Pole and wall interact, so the wall pushes the pole as the pole pushes it.
Only the pole feels a force, because the wall stays where it is and does not move.
It is a pull on the shikara, because the shikara moves away from the wall.
No force acts on the wall, because the boatman's hand never touches the wall.

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the description of the force in Column II.
Column I
1. A ring magnet held up above another ring magnet on a stick, with like poles facing
2. A bucket hauled up from a well by a rope
3. A steel clip drawn up to a magnet held above it
4. A loaded trolley shoved from behind
Column II
(a) a push, by an object in contact
(b) a pull, by an object in contact
(c) a push, by an object not in contact
(d) a pull, by an object not in contact
questions.a: 1-c, 2-b, 3-d, 4-a. Like poles repel, so the lower magnet pushes the upper one without touching; the rope pulls the bucket in contact; the magnet pulls the clip from a distance; the hands push the trolley in contact.

questions.q:
Aarav flies a kite on Makar Sankranti and feels the string tugging at his fingers.
(a) Name the object exerting this pull on his fingers.
(b) A rival's kite cuts his string. What happens at that moment to the tug on his fingers and to the string's pull on his kite? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The kite string pulls on his fingers. (b) Both forces disappear: his fingers no longer feel the tug and his kite is no longer pulled by his string, because as soon as an interaction ceases the objects no longer experience the force.
s: Names the string as the object pulling his fingers
Says both forces vanish because the interaction has ceased

questions.q: Write a short situation set in a kitchen in which (i) a pull is applied on an object, (ii) you can show that each of the two interacting objects feels a force, and (iii) the force stops when the interaction stops. Name the two interacting objects and point out where each of (i), (ii) and (iii) happens in your situation.
questions.a: Sample: Amma pulls open a stiff fridge door by its handle. (i) Her hand applies a pull on the handle. (ii) The handle and her hand interact, so she feels the handle pulling back on her fingers. (iii) When she lets go of the handle the pull on the door and the force on her fingers both stop. Interacting objects: her hand and the door handle.
s: Situation in a kitchen with a pull on an object, two interacting objects named
Shows where each object feels a force
Shows the force on both ending when the interaction ends

questions.q:
On a ride from Mysuru to a hilltop temple, three things happen to Nikhil:
Moment 1: He rides into a strong wind and has to work harder at the pedals.
Moment 2: He presses the lever of his bicycle bell near a herd of goats.
Moment 3: On the way down he stops pedalling, yet his bicycle speeds up along the slope.
For each moment, name the object that applies the force on Nikhil or on the part of his bicycle that is acted on, and say whether that force is a push or a pull.
questions.a: Moment 1: the moving air (wind) pushes against Nikhil, a push. Moment 2: Nikhil's thumb pushes the bell lever, a push. Moment 3: the Earth pulls Nikhil and the bicycle down the slope, a pull (the same 'something pulling us downhill' that the chapter later calls gravitational force).
s: Moment 1: wind on Nikhil, push
Moment 2: thumb on lever, push
Moment 3: the Earth pulling bicycle and rider, pull

questions.q: A bar magnet lies on a smooth table in Ranchi. A steel nail placed 3 cm away slides across and sticks to it. Sana writes: 'The magnet pulled the nail, but the nail did nothing to the magnet.' Which statement corrects Sana?
questions.a: The nail also pulls on the magnet; both feel a force. Whenever two objects interact, each experiences a force from the other, even when they interact without touching.
o: The nail also pulls on the magnet; both feel a force.
She is right: a nail is not a magnet, so it exerts no force.
The nail exerts a force on the magnet only once they touch.
The magnet pulls the nail, and the nail pushes the magnet away.

questions.q:
A feather drifts slowly down through still air in a classroom. The rule says at least two objects must interact for a force to act.
(a) Which object interacts with the feather to make it fall at all?
(b) Which other object interacts with the feather to make the fall slow?
questions.a: (a) The Earth, which pulls the feather down (gravitational force). (b) The air, which exerts a force of friction on objects moving through it and so opposes the feather's motion.
s: Names the Earth as the object pulling the feather down
Names the air as the object whose friction slows the fall

questions.q:
Three students wrote these definitions of force for a class poster.
Tara: 'A force is a push that makes an object move.'
Umang: 'A force is something an object has inside it, like the force inside a moving cricket ball.'
Veda: 'A force is a pull between two objects that are touching.'
(a) Point out what is wrong or missing in each definition, giving one example from the chapter that the definition cannot explain. (3)
(b) Write one definition that fixes all three faults, and give one example where a force acts without contact. (2)
questions.a: (a) Tara leaves out pulls (lifting a box is a pull) and assumes force always causes motion, but an object at rest can have forces acting on it (they balance). Umang treats force as something owned by one object, but a force results from the interaction of two objects and ends when the interaction ends (the bat's push stops once the ball leaves it). Veda leaves out pushes (pressing a balloon) and wrongly needs touching: a magnet attracts a pin from a distance. (b) A force is a push or a pull on an object resulting from the object's interaction with another object. Example without contact: a magnet attracting a steel pin, or a charged scale attracting paper bits.
s: Fault in Tara's definition with an example
Fault in Umang's definition with an example
Fault in Veda's definition with an example
A corrected definition with push or pull and interaction
A correct non-contact example

questions.q:
At a Bhopal school's Sports Day, the commentator's card lists three events.
Event P, Tug-of-war: two teams hold a rope; for the first 10 seconds the rope does not move at all.
Event Q, Shot put: an athlete pushes an iron ball away from her shoulder.
Event R, High jump: an athlete leaves the ground, rises over the bar, and comes back down onto the mat while touching nothing on the way.
(a) In Event P, name the objects that interact with the rope during the first 10 seconds and say whether they push or pull it.
(b) In Event R, name the object that brings the athlete back down while she is in the air, and the kind of force it is.
(c) Look only at the force each card describes: the teams' pull on the rope in P, her push on the ball in Q, and the force that brings her down in R. The judge needs one event for a poster titled 'A force can act between objects that are not touching.' Choose the event and explain why each of the other two does not suit this poster.
questions.a: (a) The two teams (their hands) interact with the rope and both pull it; the rope stays still because the pulls on it balance. (b) The Earth pulls her down; it is a pull that acts without contact (the gravitational force). (c) Event R. While she is in the air nothing touches her, yet the Earth pulls her down. In Event P the teams' hands grip the rope and in Event Q her hand touches the ball while pushing it, so both of these are forces by objects in contact.
s: Names both teams pulling the rope
Names the Earth pulling her down without contact
Chooses Event R and rules out P and Q because their forces need contact

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A goalkeeper who catches a fast shot and holds the ball still in her gloves has applied a force on the ball.
Reason (R): A force applied on a moving object can decrease its speed or bring it to a stop.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Catching the ball brings a moving ball to rest, which is a change in speed, and that cannot happen without a force; so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Zoya flicks her carrom striker at a coin lying still at the centre of the board. The coin slides off towards a pocket, and the striker bounces back towards Zoya, more slowly than before. What did the collision do to the striker itself?
questions.a: It changed both the striker's speed and its direction The striker now moves the other way (direction changed) and more slowly (speed changed). Both objects in an interaction experience a force, so the striker is affected too.
o: It changed both the striker's speed and its direction
It changed the striker's direction only, not its speed
It only set the striker moving from rest
Nothing, since the force acted on the coin, not the striker

questions.q: In which of these does the force produce ONLY a change in shape, with no motion started, stopped or turned?
questions.a: Squeezing a rubber ball in a fist resting on a desk Squeezing the ball only changes its shape. The kick starts motion from rest, the fielder stops a moving ball, and turning the handle changes the direction of motion.
o: Squeezing a rubber ball in a fist resting on a desk
Kicking a football that is lying still on the field
A fielder stopping a ball rolling to the boundary
Turning the handle of a moving autorickshaw

questions.q: Rohan's science diary says: 'My toy car moved along the floor at a steady speed in a straight line, then went round a curve at the same steady speed, then went straight again. No force acted on it at any time, because its speed never changed.' Show that his conclusion cannot be correct.
questions.a: Going round the curve changed the car's direction of motion. A force can change the direction of motion of an object, and none of these changes (speed, direction or shape) takes place without the action of a force. So a force must have acted on the car at least while it went round the curve; an unchanged speed does not mean no force acted.
s: Identifies that the direction of motion changed on the curve
States that a change in direction cannot happen without a force
Concludes a force acted while turning, so his reason (unchanged speed) is not enough

questions.q:
A cook in Amritsar first rolls a ball of dough into a flat chapati, then flips the chapati on the tawa with a quick jerk of her tongs: the chapati, lying still, rises, turns over and lands.
(a) Which effect of force does the rolling produce?
(b) Name any two effects of force seen during the flip.
questions.a: (a) A change in the shape of the dough. (b) Any two of: the chapati is made to move from rest; its speed changes (it rises, slows, falls); its direction of motion changes (up, then down).
s: Rolling: change in shape
Flip: any two of move from rest, change in speed, change in direction

questions.q: A batter hits a full toss that was coming straight at her. The ball flies back the way it came, faster than it arrived, and the soft ball is squashed for an instant at the moment of the hit. Of the four effects of force in the chapter (move from rest, change speed, change direction, change shape), the number seen on the ball here is ___.

A city bus in Secunderabad was tracked for five minutes.
Minute 0 to 1: stands at the bus stop, then starts and reaches 20 km/h heading east.
Minute 1 to 2: still heading east, speeds up from 20 km/h to 40 km/h.
Minute 2 to 3: keeps a steady 40 km/h heading east on a straight road.
Minute 3 to 4: keeps 40 km/h but turns at a junction until it heads north.
Minute 4 to 5: heading north, slows from 40 km/h to 0 at the next stop.
(a) For each of the five minutes, name the effect of force (if any) that the record shows. (4)
(b) In which minute does the record not prove that a force acted? Explain why the chapter's rule cannot be used to prove a force in that minute. (1)
questions.a: (a) Minute 0 to 1: the bus is made to move from rest (counted as one effect; 'change of speed' is also accepted). Minute 1 to 2: change in speed (it speeds up). Minute 3 to 4: change in direction of motion. Minute 4 to 5: change in speed (it slows to a stop). (b) Minute 2 to 3: the speed and direction stay the same and the shape does not change, so the rule 'none of these changes take place without a force' gives no evidence of a force in that minute.
s: Minute 0 to 1: move from rest (also accepted: change of speed from zero)
Minute 1 to 2: change in speed
Minute 3 to 4: change in direction
Minute 4 to 5: change in speed (stopping)
Picks minute 2 to 3 and explains that nothing the rule depends on changes

questions.q:
In a Kochi school lab, a soft clay ball is rolled slowly eastward along a long bench. In each trial, a partner does one thing to the moving ball and the students record what they see afterwards.
Trial 1: the ball is moving east, faster than before; its shape is unchanged.
Trial 2: the ball is moving north at the same speed as before; its shape is unchanged.
Trial 3: the ball is at rest, and one side of it is now flat.
Trial 4: the ball is moving west, faster than before; its shape is unchanged.
(a) Name the effect of force shown in Trial 2.
(b) Name every effect of force shown in Trial 3.
(c) A student writes 'Trial 4: change of direction.' Is her entry complete? Name every effect shown in Trial 4.
(d) The teacher wants one of these trials for a parents' evening. Visitors will arrive after the trial is over and will see only the ball as it was left on the bench. Trials 3 and 4 each show two effects. Which trial should she use, and which of its effects will the visitors still be able to see for themselves?
questions.a: (a) A change in the direction of motion. (b) The ball stops (a change in speed, to zero) and its shape changes: two effects. (c) Her entry is incomplete. The ball now moves the opposite way (change of direction) and it is faster than before (change of speed): two effects. (d) Trial 3. Changes in speed and direction are seen only while the ball is moving, so once Trial 4 is over and the ball comes to rest, nothing on the bench shows them. In Trial 3 the flattened side, the change of shape, stays and can still be seen; the stopping itself has to be told to them, since a ball at rest does not show that it was moving.
s: Trial 2: change in direction
Trial 3: stopping (change in speed) and change in shape
Trial 4: change of direction and change of speed, so the entry is incomplete
Chooses Trial 3 because only a change of shape is left to see after the trial; changes of motion leave no trace

questions.q:
Read three statements about what a force can do.
Statement 1: A ball thrown straight up slows down, stops and falls back, so a force changes both its speed and its direction of motion.
Statement 2: A force applied on an object always makes the object move.
Statement 3: Stretching a rubber band is an example of a force changing the shape of an object.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is wrong because a force can change only the shape of an object (pressing a ball held in the hand) or act on an object at rest where forces balance.
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
An autorickshaw driver in Pune applies the brake while turning the handle through a bend, so the vehicle goes from 30 km/h to 15 km/h as it turns.
(a) Name every effect of force on the autorickshaw's motion during this action.
(b) Later, on a straight road at 30 km/h, he squeezes the brake lever, but the brake cable has snapped and the autorickshaw keeps going at 30 km/h in a straight line. Did his hand's force produce any of the chapter's effects on the motion of the autorickshaw? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Two effects: a change in speed (30 km/h to 15 km/h) and a change in the direction of motion (it goes round the bend). (b) No. The autorickshaw's speed and direction do not change, so no effect on its motion appears. His hand's force moved only the lever; with the cable snapped, the lever no longer interacts with the brake, so the force does not reach the wheels.
s: Change in speed and change in direction during the braking turn
No effect on the vehicle's motion, because speed and direction are unchanged and the snapped cable breaks the interaction

questions.q: In which of these is NO change taking place that the chapter says needs a force?
questions.a: A parked scooter that stays in place all afternoon The parked scooter's speed, direction and shape do not change. Pulling away is motion from rest, going round is a change in direction, and slowing is a change in speed.
o: A parked scooter that stays in place all afternoon
A scooter pulling away from a red light as it turns green
A scooter going round a roundabout at a steady speed
A scooter slowing down at a speed breaker

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'If a toy car moving in a straight line suddenly changes its direction without slowing down or speeding up, a force must have acted on it.'
questions.a: True. A force can change the direction of motion of an object, and a change in direction does not take place without the action of a force, even when the speed stays the same.
s: States True
Explains that a change in direction alone needs a force, even at unchanged speed

questions.q:
Complete the entries for a table like the chapter's 'Different actions and their effects' for these three actions. For each, write push or pull and the effect on the object acted upon.
(i) A goalkeeper punches away a ball that is flying towards her goal.
(ii) A mechanic squeezes a tube of grease.
(iii) A child tugs a toy cart that is standing still, using a string tied to its front.
questions.a: (i) Push; it changes the direction of motion of the ball (and its speed). (ii) Push; it changes the shape of the tube. (iii) Pull; it makes the cart move from rest.
s: (i) Push, change in direction of the ball
(ii) Push, change in shape of the tube
(iii) Pull, cart made to move from rest

questions.q:
In a school match in Jaipur, a fielder dives and stops a ball that was rolling towards the boundary, then gets up and throws the ball, which was lying still in her hand, to the wicketkeeper.
(a) Which effect of force does her dive have on the ball?
(b) Which effect does her throw have on the ball, given that the ball was at rest in her hand?
questions.a: (a) It stops the ball, that is, it changes (decreases) the speed of the moving ball to zero. (b) It makes the ball move from rest.
s: Dive: stopping the ball, a change in speed
Throw: making the ball move from rest

questions.q: A student records four events. In which one did a single action produce exactly two of the chapter's effects of force on the object acted upon?
questions.a: A moving car hits a pole, stops, and its bumper is bent. Stopping is a change in speed and the bent bumper is a change in shape. The marble only starts moving from rest, the band only changes shape, and the cyclist only speeds up. A start from rest is counted as one effect, so the flicked marble shows one effect.
o: A moving car hits a pole, stops, and its bumper is bent
A still marble is flicked and rolls straight across the floor
A rubber band is stretched between two fingers and held there
A cyclist rolls downhill in a straight line, getting faster

questions.q:
A toy company in Channapatna tests three bumpers for the end of a wooden toy-car track. A toy car is run into each bumper at the same speed.
Bumper W: the car stops; the foam is left pressed in by 1 mm more after every run, and the bumper must be replaced after 20 runs. Cost Rs 10 each.
Bumper Y: the car ends up 30 cm back along the track, moving back towards the child; the bumper looks the same as before. Cost Rs 8.
Bumper Z: the car stops; the bumper looks exactly the same after every run. Cost Rs 25, lasts the life of the toy.
(a) What effect does the car's force have on Bumper W that it does not have on Bumper Z?
(b) Name the effects that Bumper Y's force has on the car's motion.
(c) The toy is expected to run about 60 times in its life. Find the total cost of bumpers for W and for Z over that time.
(d) The company does not want the car sent back towards the child. Which bumper should it choose? Justify using your answers to (a), (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) It changes W's shape (the foam stays pressed in a little more after each run); Z's shape does not change. (b) It changes the car's direction of motion (it now moves back towards the child) and its speed. (c) W: 60 / 20 = 3 bumpers, 3 x Rs 10 = Rs 30. Z: one bumper, Rs 25. (d) Bumper Z. Y is ruled out because its force reverses the car's direction and sends it back towards the child. W and Z both stop the car, but the car's force keeps changing W's shape, so it wears out and costs Rs 30 over 60 runs, while Z keeps its shape after every run and costs only Rs 25. Z is both cheaper and unchanged in shape.
s: W: the car's force changes its shape; Z keeps its shape
Y changes the car's direction (and speed)
Costs: W Rs 30 (3 bumpers), Z Rs 25
Chooses Z: rules out Y (direction) and W (shape change, higher cost)

questions.q: Plan a four-step demonstration for your class with just one football and a flat playground, so that each step shows a different effect of force from the chapter, in this order: move from rest, change of speed, change of direction, change of shape. For each step write (i) exactly what you do to the ball, (ii) whether your force is a push or a pull, and (iii) the effect the class should see. Then explain why the step showing 'change of speed' cannot be done first.
questions.a: Sample. Step 1: kick the ball lying still: push; it moves from rest. Step 2: run beside the rolling ball and tap it forward again: push; it speeds up (change in speed). Step 3: tap the moving ball from the side: push; its direction of motion changes. Step 4: hold the ball still and press it hard between the palms: push; its shape changes. A change of speed of a rolling ball needs the ball to be already moving; the ball starts at rest, so the 'move from rest' step must come first.
s: Step 1 makes the ball move from rest with a stated push or pull
Step 2 changes the speed of the moving ball
Step 3 changes the direction of motion
Step 4 changes the shape
Explains that a speed change of a moving ball needs it moving first

questions.q: Arun says: 'If nothing about an object changes, its speed, its direction and its shape all staying the same, then no force is acting on it at all.' Which point from the chapter shows the flaw in his reasoning?
questions.a: An object at rest can have forces on it that balance one another An object at rest may have forces acting on it that are balancing one another, so 'no change' does not prove 'no force'.
o: An object at rest can have forces on it that balance one another
An opened drawer shows that a force always causes some change in an object
A stretched rubber band shows that a force only changes shape
A fielder stopping a ball shows that a force only stops objects

questions.q:
Anjali glides on her skateboard along a straight road.
(a) She pushes one foot against the road and the skateboard goes faster. Which effect of force is this?
(b) She then drags the same foot on the road and slows down. Does the road's force on her foot act in the direction she is moving or opposite to it? Give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) A change (increase) in speed. (b) Opposite to her direction of motion: the dragged foot slides over the road, and friction always acts opposite to the direction in which the object is moving, which slows her down.
s: Push against the road gives a change in speed
Road's force on the dragged foot acts opposite to her motion because friction opposes motion

questions.q: Can a single hit with a racket produce all four effects of force listed in the chapter on a tennis ball that is already moving? Using the list of effects, show which of the four effects a single hit on a ball that is ALREADY moving can produce, and explain why one of them is impossible in that hit.
questions.a: A hit on a moving ball can change its speed, change its direction of motion and change its shape (the ball squashes for an instant), so up to three effects at once. It cannot 'make the object move from rest', because the ball was already moving before the hit; that effect applies only to an object at rest.
s: Lists change in speed, direction and shape as possible in one hit
Identifies 'move from rest' as the impossible one
Explains that the ball was not at rest before the hit

questions.q: Kavya pushes a heavy almirah towards the door, but it does not move at all. What can be said about friction on the almirah at that moment?
questions.a: It acts opposite to the way she is trying to move it Friction comes into play when an object moves or tries to move over another surface, and it acts opposite to the direction in which the object is moving or trying to move.
o: It acts opposite to the way she is trying to move it
There is none, because the almirah is not moving yet
It acts the same way as her push, helping her
It acts straight down, pressing it to the floor

questions.q: During a game in a Nagpur park, Arjun kicks a football from rest, it rolls across the grass and slows down, he traps it under his foot, and then his dog picks it up in its mouth. Which change in the ball's motion was NOT caused by a muscular force?
questions.a: The ball slowing as it rolls on the grass. The slowing is caused by friction between the ball and the grass. The kick, the trap and the dog's lift all come from the action of muscles.
o: The ball slowing as it rolls on the grass
The ball starting to move when kicked
The ball being lifted in the dog's mouth
The ball stopping when Arjun traps it underfoot

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the idea in Column II that explains it.
Column I
1. A high-speed train is given a long, pointed front
2. A bicycle that stops being pedalled comes to rest sooner on a rough road than on a smooth one
3. A heavy sack does not budge when a child pushes it gently
4. Food is moved along the alimentary canal
Column II
(a) friction acts even when an object only tries to move
(b) air exerts friction on objects moving through it
(c) friction is greater on rougher surfaces
(d) muscular force acts inside the body
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-a, 4-d. The train's shape reduces friction due to air; the rough road gives greater friction; the still sack is being made to try to move, so friction opposes the push; muscular force pushes food through the alimentary canal.

questions.q:
A shepherd in Himachal Pradesh steers a stray sheep back to the flock by tapping it with a long stick; his hand never touches the sheep.
(a) Is the force on the sheep a contact force or a non-contact force?
(b) Explain why, even though his hand never touches the sheep.
questions.a: (a) A contact force (the muscular force of his arm acts on the sheep through the stick). (b) The contact needed for a contact force can be direct, using our hands, or indirect, through a stick or a rope; here the stick touches the sheep, so it is indirect contact.
s: Classifies it as a contact force
Explains that contact can be indirect through a stick

questions.q:
Class 8 students in Indore placed the same lunch box on five surfaces and gave it the same push each time, so it started at the same speed. They measured how far it slid before stopping.
Glass: 92 cm | Ceramic tile: 75 cm | Wood: 54 cm | Cloth: 30 cm | Sand: 8 cm
(a) On which surface was the force of friction the greatest? Explain how the data shows this.
(b) Why was it important that the push was the same in every trial?
(c) A student says, 'Glass looks perfectly smooth, so there is no friction on glass; the box just ran out of push.' Use the data and the chapter to show that friction did act on the glass.
(d) Predict a range for the distance the box would slide on a mat that is rougher than wood but smoother than cloth. Give your reasoning.
questions.a: (a) Sand: the box stopped after only 8 cm, the shortest distance, so the opposing force of friction was greatest there. (b) If the pushes differed, the box would start at different speeds and the distance could change because of the push, not the surface; only with the same push can the distances be blamed on the surfaces. (c) The box slowed and stopped after 92 cm, and a change in speed needs a force; the force came from the glass surface in contact, so friction acted. Even surfaces that appear smooth have many minute irregularities that lock into those of the box; on glass the friction is only smaller, which is why the box went farthest there. (d) Between 30 cm and 54 cm: friction is greater on rougher surfaces, so the mat stops the box sooner than wood (less than 54 cm) but later than cloth (more than 30 cm).
s: Sand, because the shortest slide means the greatest friction
The same push keeps the starting speed the same so only the surface changes
The box stopped on glass, so a force (friction) acted; smooth-looking glass still has minute irregularities
Predicts between 30 cm and 54 cm with the roughness reasoning

questions.q:
On a cycle trip near Nashik, Omkar notes five things. For each one, name the force involved, say whether it is a contact force, and explain the observation. (Be careful: not every force here is a contact force.)
1. On flat ground, pedalling across a stretch of loose gravel needs more effort than on smooth tar.
2. When he stops pedalling on a flat road, the bicycle slows down and stops.
3. Coming down a slope without pedalling, the bicycle keeps getting faster.
4. Racing down that slope on a still day, he feels the air pressing against his face and chest.
5. Even when he rests under a tree, his heart keeps beating.
questions.a: 1. Friction, a contact force; it is greater on rough surfaces, and gravel is rougher, so its irregularities lock more and oppose the wheels' motion more. 2. Friction between the tyres and the road, a contact force acting opposite to the motion, decreases the speed until the bicycle stops. 3. Gravitational force: the Earth pulls the bicycle and rider down the slope; it is NOT a contact force, as it acts without contact. 4. Friction exerted by the air, a contact force; air exerts friction on objects moving through it, opposing his motion. 5. Muscular force inside the body, a contact force: the expansion and contraction of the heart muscles makes blood circulate.
s: 1: friction, contact, greater on the rougher gravel
2: friction, contact, opposite to motion, reduces speed to zero
3: gravitational force of the Earth, identified as non-contact
4: friction exerted by air, contact, opposing motion
5: muscular force of heart muscles, contact, inside the body

questions.q: A line in Leela's notebook reads: 'When a pair of bullocks pulls a plough through a field, their muscular force on the plough is a contact force, even though the bullocks never touch the plough blade cutting the soil.' Her teacher writes 'Check this.' Is the line right, wrong or partly right? Justify.
questions.a: Right. The bullocks' force comes from their muscles, so it is muscular force. Muscular force is a contact force, and the contact can be indirect, through a rope or a stick (here the yoke and the pole); the bullocks are connected to the plough through these, so it is still a contact force though they never touch the blade.
s: Verdict: right
Identifies the force as muscular force, a contact force
Explains indirect contact through the yoke, pole or rope

questions.q: Given the same push each time, a toy block slid 25 cm on a jute mat, 6 cm on gravel and 70 cm on marble. The surface that exerted the least friction on the block was ___.
questions.a: marble

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'An aeroplane flying high in the sky faces no friction, because there is no solid surface for it to rub against.'
questions.a: False. Air, water and other liquids also exert a force of friction on objects moving through them; that is why aeroplanes are designed with specific shapes to reduce the friction due to the air around them.
s: States False
Explains that air exerts friction on objects moving through it, hence the special shapes

questions.q: At a pond in Kolkata, a frog leaps off a lily pad, a kingfisher flaps up from a branch, and a fish darts away from a heron. Which statement about the force that starts each animal moving is correct?
questions.a: All three use muscular force, a contact force. Animals, birds, fish and insects use muscular force for movement; the force comes from muscles acting on the body and on what it pushes against.
o: All three use muscular force, a contact force
Only the frog uses muscular force; birds float on air
The fish starts moving because of friction from the water
They are non-contact forces, as nothing touches them

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A loaded bullock cart rolls on a little and then stops after the bullocks stop pulling it.
Reason (R): Humans have used the muscular force of animals to carry out many tasks for a long time.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. A is true (friction opposite to its motion stops the cart) and R is true, but R does not explain why the cart stops; friction does.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A kingfisher dives into a pond and swims a short way under the water to catch a fish.
(a) Which force does the kingfisher use to beat its wings and dive?
(b) Which force from the water opposes its motion under water, and why does that happen?
questions.a: (a) Muscular force (of its wing and body muscles). (b) Friction from the water: water exerts a force of friction on objects moving through it, acting opposite to the bird's motion.
s: Muscular force for flying and diving
Friction exerted by water opposing motion through it

questions.q:
Riya sits still at her desk eating a banana. She lists four things happening to her body:
1. Her jaws chew the banana.
2. The chewed banana moves along her alimentary canal.
3. Blood keeps circulating through her body.
4. Her body presses down on the chair because the Earth pulls her.
She says all four are caused by muscular force. Which three are muscular force, why is the fourth not, and why does her sitting 'still' not mean that no muscular force is acting?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3 are muscular force: the jaw muscles chew, muscular force pushes food through the alimentary canal during digestion, and the heart muscles expand and contract to circulate blood. 4 is not: the Earth's pull is the gravitational force, a non-contact force, not the action of her muscles. Muscular force acts whenever muscles contract and elongate, including inside the body, so it keeps acting even when her body as a whole does not move.
s: Names chewing, moving food along the canal and circulating blood as muscular force
Says the Earth's pull is gravitational force, not muscular (and non-contact)
Explains that muscles inside the body keep working while she is still

questions.q:
A tonga in Agra is pulled by one horse along two routes. The driver notes:
On smooth asphalt, if the horse stops pulling, the tonga rolls on for 9 m before stopping.
On a sandy riverside track, if the horse stops pulling, the tonga stops after 2 m.
(a) The horse is joined to the tonga by straps and wooden shafts. What kind of force does the horse apply on the tonga, and is it a contact force?
(b) Which force stops the tonga when the horse stops pulling, and in which direction does it act?
(c) Use the chapter's explanation of this force to say why the tonga stops sooner on sand.
(d) Must the horse keep pulling once the tonga is moving along the asphalt at a steady speed? Decide, using the data and your answer to (b).
questions.a: (a) Muscular force; a contact force, the contact being indirect through the straps and shafts. (b) Friction, acting opposite to the tonga's direction of motion. (c) Friction is greater on rougher surfaces: the sand's irregularities lock more with the wheels, so the opposing force is larger and the tonga stops in 2 m instead of 9 m. (d) Yes. Friction keeps acting opposite to the motion even on asphalt; the data shows that when the pull stops the tonga slows and stops within 9 m, so the horse must keep pulling to keep it moving.
s: Muscular force, contact through straps and shafts
Friction acting opposite to the motion
Rougher sand gives greater friction, so a shorter roll
Decides yes, because friction acts throughout and the tonga stops without the pull

questions.q:
For years a farmer in Punjab ploughed his field with a pair of bullocks joined to the plough by a yoke and a wooden pole. He now pulls the same plough with a tractor, joined to it by a steel bar.
(a) Is the bullocks' force on the plough a muscular force, a contact force, or both?
(b) Is the tractor's force on the plough muscular? Is it a contact force? Give a reason for each.
questions.a: (a) Both: it comes from the action of the bullocks' muscles, so it is muscular force, and it acts through the yoke and pole touching the plough, so it is a contact force (indirect contact). (b) It is not muscular, because no muscles are acting; the tractor is a machine. It is still a contact force, because it acts only through the steel bar in contact with the plough. Not every contact force is muscular.
s: Bullocks: muscular and contact (through yoke and pole)
Tractor: not muscular (no muscles) but still a contact force through the bar

questions.q: In a Madurai temple, a girl rings a large bell by pulling a rope tied to its clapper. Her hand never touches the clapper. Which statement about the force on the clapper is correct?
questions.a: It is a contact force, acting through the rope. Contact can be direct, using our hands, or indirect, through a stick or rope; her muscular force reaches the clapper through the rope.
o: It is a contact force, acting through the rope
It is a non-contact force, since her hand never touches it
It is muscular force acting from a distance, without contact
It is friction, since the rope rubs against the clapper

questions.q: Design a fair test to find out which of three shapes made from identical A4 sheets of paper (a flat sheet, a cone, and a tightly crumpled ball) faces the most friction from the air while falling. You have a stopwatch and a staircase. Write five steps that cover: what you keep the same, how you release each shape, what you measure, how you make your result reliable, and how you will decide which shape faces the most air friction.
questions.a: 1. Use identical sheets of the same paper so each shape has the same amount of paper; only the shape changes. 2. Drop each shape from the same height (the same step), releasing it from rest without throwing it. 3. Measure the time each shape takes to reach the floor. 4. Repeat each drop three times and take the usual time, so one bad drop does not decide it. 5. The shape that takes the longest to fall faces the most friction from the air, since air exerts friction on objects moving through it and opposes their motion; shape changes how much friction acts.
s: Keeps the paper the same so only the shape changes
Same height and release from rest each time
Measures the time to fall
Repeats the drops for reliability
Decides that the slowest fall means the most air friction, with the reason

questions.q:
In Ladakh, Tsering pulls a loaded sledge across flat snow with a rope.
(a) Name two contact forces acting on the sledge while he pulls it, and give the direction of each.
(b) The rope snaps. Which of the two forces stops acting at once, and which keeps acting until the sledge stops? Give a reason for each.
questions.a: (a) The muscular pull of Tsering through the rope, forward (in the direction he pulls), and friction from the snow, backward (opposite to the sledge's motion). (b) His pull stops at once, because the rope no longer connects him to the sledge, so the interaction has ceased. Friction keeps acting, opposite to the motion, as long as the sledge slides over the snow, so it slows the sledge to a stop.
s: Pull through the rope forward, friction from the snow backward
Pull ends when the interaction ends; friction acts while the sledge slides and stops it

questions.q: After a player hits it, a hockey puck slides across a dry ground and stops on its own after 8 m, though no player touches it again. In three linked steps, explain how you can conclude that a force acted on the puck after the hit, which force it was, and in which direction it acted.
questions.a: 1. The puck's speed decreased to zero, and a change in speed cannot happen without a force, so a force acted on it after the hit. 2. The only thing touching the puck was the ground, so the force acted between the surfaces of the puck and the ground in contact: friction. 3. Friction acts opposite to the direction of motion, so it acted backwards, opposite to the way the puck was sliding.
s: A change in speed shows a force acted
The force between puck and ground in contact is friction
Friction acts opposite to the puck's motion

questions.q:
Read three statements about contact forces.
Statement 1: Friction can act on an object that is not moving at all, if someone is pushing it.
Statement 2: A sheet of glass that looks perfectly smooth still exerts friction on a box sliding over it.
Statement 3: The muscles that push food along the alimentary canal produce a force that acts by contact.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1, 2 and 3. Friction acts when an object moves or tries to move; surfaces that appear smooth still have many minute irregularities (the box on glass still stops); and muscular force is a contact force, also inside the body.
o: Statements 1, 2 and 3
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Two ring magnets are slipped onto an upright pencil; the upper one stays floating about 2 cm above the lower one.
(a) What does this tell you about the poles of the two magnets that face each other?
(b) Both magnets are now taken off, each is turned upside down, and they are put back in the same order. Will the upper magnet still float? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The facing poles are like poles (north facing north, or south facing south), which repel each other and hold the upper magnet up without contact. (b) Yes. Turning both magnets over swaps both facing poles, so if north faced north before, now south faces south; the facing poles are still alike, so they still repel and the upper magnet still floats.
s: Facing poles are like poles, which repel
Predicts it still floats because the facing poles are still alike after both are turned

questions.q: A bar magnet X hangs freely. When the north pole of X is brought near end P of another bar magnet Y, X swings away. What will happen when the north pole of X is brought near the other end, Q, of magnet Y?
questions.a: X will swing towards end Q X is repelled by P, so P is a north pole (like poles repel); the other end Q is then a south pole, and unlike poles attract.
o: X will swing towards end Q
X will swing away from end Q as well
X will neither move towards nor away from Q
X will move towards Q only if they touch

questions.q:
Students in Lucknow test charges. Their teacher reminds them that a pull can also happen between a charged and an uncharged object, so only a push is sure evidence of like charges.
They rub balloons A and B, one after the other, with the same woollen cloth W, and rub a plastic straw S with a polythene sheet. They record:
Observation 1: A and B, hung near each other, move apart.
Observation 2: W, brought near A, pulls A towards it.
Observation 3: S, brought near A, pushes A away.
(a) Why do A and B move apart?
(b) How does the charge on W compare with the charge on A? Give the reason.
(c) From Observation 3, how does the charge on S compare with the charge on A?
(d) Predict what will happen when W is brought near S. Justify by linking your answers to (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) A and B were charged in the same way, so they carry like charges, and like charges repel. (b) W carries the opposite kind of charge to A, because when two objects are rubbed together both get charged with opposite kinds of charge. (c) S carries the same kind of charge as A, because two objects repel only if they carry like charges. (d) W and S will attract each other: W is opposite to A, and S is like A, so W and S carry unlike charges, and unlike charges attract.
s: A and B carry like charges, which repel
W has the opposite charge because rubbing charges both objects oppositely
S has the same charge as A because repulsion needs like charges
Predicts attraction between W and S by chaining (b) and (c)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A balloon rubbed with a woollen cloth can pull small bits of paper towards it without touching them.
Reason (R): When a balloon is rubbed with a woollen cloth, only the balloon gets charged; the cloth stays uncharged.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. A is true: a charged object attracts uncharged paper bits without contact. R is false: both the rubbing and the rubbed object get charged, with opposite kinds of charge.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A student finds an unlabelled object that pulls things towards it without touching them. Which observation shows that its force is magnetic and not electrostatic?
questions.a: It pulls iron filings but not small bits of paper. A magnet attracts only magnetic materials such as iron, while a charged object also attracts uncharged paper bits.
o: It pulls iron filings but not small bits of paper
It pulls both small bits of paper and iron filings
It pushes another such object away across a gap
Its pull acts across a 2 cm gap without contact

questions.q: Two ring magnets on an upright stick have like poles facing, so the upper one floats. Only the upper magnet is taken off, turned upside down and put back on the stick. Write push or pull: the force of the lower magnet on the upper one is now a ___.
questions.a: pull

questions.q: On a school quiz show, a contestant answers: 'A magnet attracts everything that is placed near it, and a rubbed balloon attracts only magnetic materials.' Is the answer right, wrong or partly right? Test each half of it against the chapter.
questions.a: Wrong, in both halves. First half: a magnet attracts only objects made of magnetic materials, not everything. Second half: a rubbed (charged) balloon attracts uncharged objects of certain materials such as small pieces of paper, which are not magnetic materials, so its attraction is not limited to magnetic materials.
s: Verdict: wrong
Corrects the first half: a magnet attracts only magnetic materials
Corrects the second half: a charged balloon attracts non-magnetic things like paper

questions.q:
Two students explain why small bits of paper jump up to a plastic scale that has just been rubbed with polythene.
Explanation 1: 'Rubbing turned the scale into a magnet.'
Explanation 2: 'Rubbing built up static charges on the scale, and a charged object attracts uncharged paper without contact.'
The class also observes: a bar magnet does not pull the same paper bits, and the rubbed scale does not pull a steel pin.
(a) Which explanation do the observations support? (1)
(b) Use the bar magnet observation to argue against Explanation 1. (1)
(c) Use the steel pin observation to argue against Explanation 1. (1)
(d) Name the force acting on the paper and say why it is called a non-contact force. (1)
(e) Predict what two such rubbed scales, hung near each other, would do, and give the reason. (1)
questions.a: (a) Explanation 2. (b) A magnet attracts objects made of magnetic materials; the bar magnet does not pull the paper, so paper is not a magnetic material and a 'magnet' scale could not pull it. (c) A magnet would attract a steel pin; the rubbed scale does not, so it is not behaving like a magnet. (d) Electrostatic force, the force exerted by a charged body on another charged or uncharged body; it acts without the scale touching the paper, so it is a non-contact force. (e) They would repel each other: both are charged in the same way, so they carry like charges, and like charges repel.
s: Chooses Explanation 2
Bar magnet ignores paper, so paper is not magnetic
Scale ignores the steel pin, so it is not a magnet
Electrostatic force, acting without contact
Predicts repulsion because of like charges

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'The electromagnet of a scrapyard crane lifts iron scrap by magnetic force, not by electrostatic force, even though it works on electricity.'
questions.a: True. Electromagnets behave like magnets, so the force they exert on iron (a magnetic material) is magnetic force. Electrostatic force is the force exerted by a charged body, such as a rubbed balloon, through static charges; using electricity does not make the crane's force electrostatic.
s: States True
Explains that an electromagnet behaves like a magnet, so its force is magnetic, not the force of static charges

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: A magnet exerts a force on an iron nail only when the nail is touching it.
Statement 2: The Earth pulls a falling coconut all the way down even though the Earth never touches the coconut while it falls.
Statement 3: Unlike magnetic poles attract each other, and unlike charges also attract each other.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is wrong because a magnet exerts a force on a magnetic material without being in contact with it (magnetic force is a non-contact force).
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Lalit holds a bar magnet under a wooden table top and moves it about. A steel paper clip lying on top of the table follows the magnet around.
(a) Which force moves the clip, and which object exerts it?
(b) Mitali says, 'The table touches both the magnet and the clip, so this is a contact force.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Magnetic force, exerted by the magnet on the steel clip (a magnetic material). (b) No. The force on the clip is exerted by the magnet, not by the table, and the magnet and the clip are never in contact; a magnet can exert a force on a magnetic material from a distance, so it is a non-contact force. The table only happens to lie between them.
s: Magnetic force exerted by the magnet on the clip
Not a contact force: the magnet, not the table, exerts it and the magnet never touches the clip

questions.q: Ritu drops a steel ball from 50 cm straight above a strong magnet lying on the floor. Which statement about the forces on the ball while it falls is correct?
questions.a: The Earth and the magnet both pull it down, neither by contact. Gravitational force pulls the ball towards the Earth and magnetic force pulls the steel ball towards the magnet; both are non-contact forces acting on it during the fall.
o: The Earth and the magnet both pull it down, neither by contact
Only the Earth pulls it, since a magnet acts only when touching
The magnet pushes it up, since magnetic force is non-contact
The Earth's pull acts on it only after it lands on the magnet

questions.q:
Kiran holds a bar magnet at different heights above a heap of steel pins and records how many pins jump up to it.
Height 6 cm: 0 pins | Height 3 cm: 2 pins | Height 1 cm: 9 pins
(a) Name the force that lifts the pins.
(b) What does the record show about whether this force needs contact?
(c) Kiran writes in her conclusion: 'At 6 cm the magnet exerts no force on the pins at all.' Does her record prove this? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Magnetic force. (b) Pins jump up while the magnet is still 3 cm and 1 cm away, so the force acts without contact; it is a non-contact force. (c) No. The record shows only that no pin jumped up at 6 cm. A pull that was too weak to lift a whole pin off the heap would leave the same record, so '0 pins' does not prove that no force acted; her conclusion claims more than her data shows.
s: Magnetic force
Pins lifted from a distance show a non-contact force
Says the record does not prove zero force: no pin lifting is not the same as no force

questions.q:
A charged balloon is held 3 cm above a small bit of paper lying on a desk, and the paper jumps up to the balloon.
(a) Name the two non-contact forces acting on the paper just before it jumps, and give the direction of each.
(b) Two charged balloons can push each other apart. Explain why the Earth's force on the paper can never become a push in the same way.
questions.a: (a) Electrostatic force from the charged balloon, upward towards the balloon (an attraction); and gravitational force from the Earth, downward. (b) Gravitational force is always an attractive force, unlike magnetic or electrostatic force, which can be attractive or repulsive; so the Earth can only pull the paper, never push it away.
s: Electrostatic force upward and gravitational force downward
Gravity is always attractive, while electrostatic force can attract or repel

questions.q:
A toy at a Pune science fair has three ring magnets A, B and C slipped onto an upright wooden rod. Each ring magnet has a north pole on one flat face and a south pole on the other. A rests on the base; B floats 1.2 cm above A; C floats 2.0 cm above B. The face of A that points up is its north pole.
(a) Which poles face each other in the gap between A and B?
(b) Which pole of B points up, and which pole of C points down?
(c) A child wants C to stick to B while B still floats above A, and is allowed to turn over just one magnet. Which magnet should she turn over? Show why turning over either of the other two does not work.
questions.a: (a) North faces north (like poles, which repel and hold B up). (b) B's lower face is north, so its upper face is south; C floats above B, so C's lower face must also be south. (c) Turn over C: its lower face becomes north, facing B's south, so they attract and C sticks to B, while the A-B gap is unchanged and B still floats. Turning over B makes its lower face south, facing A's north, so B is pulled down onto A (it no longer floats). Turning over A makes A's upper face south, facing B's north, so B drops onto A, while C still floats above B.
s: North faces north between A and B
B's top is south and C's bottom is south
Chooses C and rules out turning B and A with the pole reasoning

questions.q:
The chapter says that attraction and repulsion between objects are also a form of push and pull, that is, a force.
(a) A plastic straw rubbed with polythene is held above some paper bits, which jump up to it. Is the straw's force on the paper a push or a pull? Why?
(b) A bar magnet lies on two round pencils. When the north end of a second bar magnet is brought near its north end, the first magnet rolls away. Is the force on it a push or a pull? Why?
questions.a: (a) A pull: the charged straw attracts the uncharged paper bits, and attraction is a pull. (b) A push: like poles (north and north) repel, and repulsion is a push.
s: Straw on paper: pull, because a charged object attracts uncharged paper
Magnet: push, because like poles repel

questions.q:
Three bars, X, Y and Z, look exactly alike. Two of them are magnets and one is a plain iron bar. The students use this fact: a plain iron bar is attracted by a magnet but is never pushed away by it. They test ends in pairs.
X with Y: of the four ways of bringing an end of X near an end of Y, two push apart and two pull together.
X with Z: every pair of ends pulls together.
Y with Z: every pair of ends pulls together.
(a) Which two bars are the magnets? Explain using the repulsion. (2)
(b) Which bar is the plain iron bar, and why does it pull together with every end it meets? (1)
(c) Why could the students not identify the magnets from attraction alone? (1)
(d) The end of X marked N is brought near end K of Y, and they push apart. Which pole is end K? (1)
questions.a: (a) X and Y. Only like poles of two magnets push each other apart, and an iron bar is never pushed away, so the pair that showed a push must both be magnets. (b) Z: a magnet attracts objects made of magnetic materials, so either end of X or Y pulls Z, whichever end of Z is used. (c) Attraction happens between unlike poles of two magnets and also between a magnet and a plain iron bar, so a pull does not tell which kind of object is involved. (d) K is a north pole, because like poles repel.
s: Identifies X and Y as magnets from the repulsion
Z is the iron bar, attracted by any pole
Attraction occurs both between magnets and with iron, so it cannot identify a magnet
Y's end is a north pole

questions.q: Which force can act between two objects that are 5 cm apart AND push them away from each other?
questions.a: Magnetic force between two like poles Gravity acts without contact but is always attractive; friction and muscular force need contact. Like magnetic poles repel without touching.
o: Magnetic force between two like poles
Gravitational force of the Earth on a ball
Friction between a box and the floor
Muscular force of an arm on a door

questions.q: In which of these is electrostatic force the correct explanation of what happens?
questions.a: Paper bits leaping up to a rubbed plastic straw A plastic straw rubbed with polythene is charged and attracts uncharged paper bits without contact. The compass and the nail involve magnetic force; the sliding coin is stopped by friction.
o: Paper bits leaping up to a rubbed plastic straw
A compass needle turning when a magnet comes near
An iron nail sliding up to a bar magnet
A coin sliding to a stop on a wooden table

questions.q: Read this record: 'Object P pulled object Q towards it from 2 cm away, and P also pushed object R away from 2 cm away. P, Q and R were never touched by each other.' Describe a real situation, using only electrostatic force, that would give exactly this record. Say what P, Q and R are and how each was prepared, and explain each observation.
questions.a: Sample: P is a balloon rubbed with a woollen cloth; Q is a few small bits of paper (not rubbed); R is a second balloon rubbed with the same kind of woollen cloth in the same way. P is charged, so it attracts the uncharged paper bits Q without contact. R is charged in the same way as P, so P and R carry like charges and repel each other without contact.
s: Chooses a charged P and an uncharged Q, explaining the pull
Chooses R charged the same way as P, explaining the push
States how each object was prepared (rubbed or not) consistently

questions.q: Three bar magnets lie on a table. End A of magnet 1 pushes away end C of magnet 2. End C pulls towards end E of magnet 3, and end E is marked N. Write north or south: end A is a ___ pole.
questions.a: south

questions.q: Meera tosses a coin straight up with her thumb and catches it again at the same height. Which describes the coin's speed from the moment it leaves her thumb until she catches it?
questions.a: It decreases, is zero for a moment, then increases Under the Earth's pull, an object thrown vertically up slows down, stops momentarily at the top, changes direction, and speeds up while coming down.
o: It decreases, is zero for a moment, then increases
It stays the same all the way up and down
It increases going up and decreases coming down
It decreases going up and stays zero after the top

questions.q: On the Earth, a lunch box hung from a spring balance pulls its newton scale to 4.5 N. The balance's mass scale is marked on the assumption that 1 kg weighs 10 N on the Earth. Write the number only: the mass scale points to ___ g.

A science club in Bengaluru imagines a shop at a base on the Moon. It plans to take a spring balance from the Earth. The balance has a newton scale and, beside it, a mass scale in kilograms that was marked assuming the balance would be used on the Earth, where 1 kg weighs 10 N. On the Moon, a 1 kg mass weighs 1.6 N. Take the weight to be in proportion to the mass (2 kg weighs twice as much as 1 kg at the same place). A packet of rice packed on the Earth has a mass of 2 kg.
(a) What is the packet's mass on the Moon? Give the reason.
(b) What will the newton scale read for the packet on the Moon?
(c) What will the mass scale read for the packet on the Moon?
(d) The shopkeeper must sell rice by mass with this balance on the Moon. Should she read the mass scale, or the newton scale and work out the mass? Decide, using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) 2 kg: mass is the amount of matter in an object and remains the same at every place. (b) 2 x 1.6 = 3.2 N. (c) The mass scale assumes 10 N for every 1 kg, so 3.2 N shows as 3.2 / 10 = 0.32 kg. (d) She should read the newton scale and divide by 1.6 N per kg (3.2 / 1.6 = 2 kg). The mass scale was marked for the Earth's pull, so on the Moon it would show 0.32 kg for 2 kg of rice, a wrong mass.
s: Mass stays 2 kg, as mass does not change with place
Newton scale reads 3.2 N
Mass scale reads 0.32 kg
Chooses the newton scale with division by 1.6 N per kg, because the mass scale is marked for the Earth

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Gravitational force is a non-contact force.
Reason (R): Gravitational force is always an attractive force.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true, but gravity is called non-contact because it acts without contact with the object it attracts; being always attractive is a different property, which is what sets it apart from magnetic and electrostatic force.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A Chennai school's spring balance measures from 0 to 20 N. Its bigger marks are at every 2 N, and between two bigger marks there are 10 equal small divisions.
(a) What is the smallest weight this balance can read? (1)
(b) A pencil box pulls the pointer to 3 small divisions past the 4 N mark. What is its weight? (1)
(c) Kavin wants to hang his school bag, which is about 45 N, from this balance. Should he? Give the reason. (1)
(d) Write the pencil box's weight correctly, and say why the statement 'the pencil box weighs 460 g' does not give a weight in the scientific sense. (1)
(e) If this balance were taken to the Moon, would it show a smaller, equal or larger reading for the same pencil box? Why, though the pencil box itself has not changed? (1)
questions.a: (a) 2 N / 10 = 0.2 N. (b) 4 + 3 x 0.2 = 4.6 N. (c) No: 45 N is more than the 20 N maximum, and an object heavier than the maximum the balance can measure may damage it; he should use a balance with a larger range. (d) 4.6 N. Weight is a force and its SI unit is the newton; the gram is a unit of mass, so '460 g' states a mass, not a weight. (e) Smaller. Weight is the pull of the Earth or Moon on the object; the Moon pulls it with a smaller force (1.6 N instead of 10 N per kg), while its mass stays the same.
s: Least count 0.2 N
Pencil box reads 4.6 N
Rejects the 45 N bag because it exceeds the 20 N range and may damage the balance
4.6 N; gram is a unit of mass, weight is a force in newton
Smaller on the Moon because the Moon's pull is weaker while the mass is unchanged

questions.q: A ration shop's list says 'Weight of wheat bag: 10 kg'. On the Earth a 1 kg mass weighs about 10 N. Which statement uses the terms correctly?
questions.a: Its mass is 10 kg; its weight on the Earth is about 100 N Kilogram is the unit of mass and the newton is the unit of weight; 10 kg on the Earth weighs about 10 x 10 = 100 N. Everyday language says 'weight' for mass, which is not correct scientifically.
o: Its mass is 10 kg; its weight on the Earth is about 100 N
Its weight is 10 kg; its mass on the Earth is about 100 N
Its weight is 10 kg both on the Earth and on the Moon
Its mass is 10 N, since mass is also a kind of force

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'A spring balance with a scale in grams measures the mass of an object directly, so its gram reading would stay correct even if the balance were used on the Moon.'
questions.a: False. The spring stretches because of the pull of the Earth on the object, so a spring balance measures weight (a force). Its gram scale is only marked on the assumption that the balance is used on the Earth; the mass is found indirectly from the weight. On the Moon the pull is much weaker, so the stretch is smaller and the gram scale would show too small a mass.
s: States False
Explains the spring responds to the pull (weight); the gram scale assumes the Earth's pull, so it reads wrong on the Moon

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: An object dropped from a height and an object thrown straight up both move along straight vertical paths.
Statement 2: The Earth pulls a heavy stone and a light feather with the same force, since gravity acts on every object.
Statement 3: An object's mass on Jupiter is about two and a half times its mass on the Earth, because 1 kg weighs 25.4 N there instead of 10 N.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only. Statement 2 is wrong: the Earth pulls different objects with different forces (a spring is stretched by different amounts), so their weights differ. Statement 3 is wrong: the weight changes from planet to planet but the mass stays the same.
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only

questions.q:
On the Earth a 1 kg mass weighs 10 N, and on Venus it weighs 9 N. Take the weight to be in proportion to the mass (2 kg weighs twice as much as 1 kg at the same place). 
(a) What would a 6 kg suitcase weigh on Venus?
(b) Explain why a spring balance would show a smaller reading for the suitcase on Venus than on the Earth, while its mass is still 6 kg.
questions.a: (a) 6 x 9 = 54 N. (b) The spring balance measures weight, the gravitational pull on the suitcase; Venus pulls it a little less strongly than the Earth (54 N against 60 N), but the amount of matter in the suitcase, its mass, does not change.
s: Weight on Venus 54 N
Reading is the planet's pull, which is weaker on Venus, while the mass is unchanged

questions.q: A 5 kg dumbbell is taken from Delhi to a base on the Moon. On the Earth 1 kg weighs 10 N and on the Moon 1 kg weighs 1.6 N. Take the weight to be in proportion to the mass (2 kg weighs twice as much as 1 kg at the same place). Using the dumbbell, differentiate between mass and weight by stating its mass and its weight in each place.
questions.a: Delhi: mass 5 kg, weight 5 x 10 = 50 N. Moon: mass still 5 kg, weight 5 x 1.6 = 8 N. Mass (in kg) is the amount of matter and stays the same; weight (in N) is the gravitational pull and changes from place to place.
s: Mass 5 kg in both places
Weight 50 N in Delhi and 8 N on the Moon

questions.q:
A box has a mass of 2 kg. A 1 kg mass weighs 1.6 N on the Moon, 3.8 N on Mars, 9 N on Venus and 25.4 N on Jupiter. Take the weight to be in proportion to the mass. Match each place in Column I with the box's weight there in Column II.
Column I
1. Moon
2. Mars
3. Venus
4. Jupiter
Column II
(a) 50.8 N
(b) 18 N
(c) 7.6 N
(d) 3.2 N
Three objects are hung one at a time from the same spring. The stone stretches it by 2 cm, the tiffin box by 5 cm and the pencil box by 3 cm. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: The Earth pulls the tiffin box with the greatest force The spring stretches because of the Earth's pull on the hanging object; a bigger stretch means a bigger pull, that is, a greater weight.
o: The Earth pulls the tiffin box with the greatest force
The Earth pulls all three equally; only the stretch differs
The stone has the greatest weight, as it is the hardest
The pencil box weighs most, as its stretch is in the middle

questions.q: A shopkeeper tells a customer: 'This bag's weight stays exactly the same at every place on the Earth; it changes only if you take it to another planet.' Is the shopkeeper right, wrong or partly right? Justify each part of your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The shopkeeper is right that weight changes on other planets: the gravitational force can be very different there (1 kg weighs 10 N on the Earth but 3.8 N on Mars). The shopkeeper is not right that it is exactly the same everywhere on the Earth: the gravitational force can vary very slightly from place to place on the Earth, so weight stays almost, not exactly, the same.
s: Verdict: partly right
Confirms that weight differs on other planets, with an example
Corrects 'exactly the same on Earth' to 'almost the same', as gravity varies slightly

questions.q:
A ball is thrown straight up from a rooftop ledge in Jodhpur. A camera notes its height above the ledge every 0.2 s:
0 m, 1.4 m, 2.4 m, 3.0 m, 3.2 m, 3.0 m, 2.4 m, 1.4 m, 0 m.
(a) At which height is the ball momentarily at rest? Give the reason from the data.
(b) How does the distance moved in each 0.2 s change on the way up and on the way down? What does this tell you about the ball's speed?
(c) Name the force responsible for these changes and explain why the ball's direction of motion reverses.
questions.a: (a) At 3.2 m, the highest point: it rises to 3.2 m and then starts coming down, so it stops momentarily there. (b) Going up, the distances are 1.4, 1.0, 0.6 and 0.2 m, getting smaller, so its speed decreases; coming down they are 0.2, 0.6, 1.0 and 1.4 m, getting larger, so its speed increases. (c) The Earth's gravitational force, which always pulls the ball downward; it slows the ball until it stops at the top, and because the pull is still downward the ball then moves down with increasing speed.
s: 3.2 m, the top, where it stops for a moment
