Distances shrink going up and grow coming down, so speed decreases then increases
Gravity always pulling down slows, stops and reverses the ball

questions.q:
Two ring magnets can make one magnet float above the other without any support.
(a) Could the Earth's gravitational force alone ever hold a stationary object floating above the ground in the same way?
(b) Give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) No. (b) The magnets float the upper magnet by repulsion (a push between like poles), but gravitational force is always an attractive force, unlike magnetic force; it can only pull objects towards the Earth, never push them away.
s: Says no
Explains that gravity is always attractive while the magnets float it by repulsion

questions.q:
A student made a short video, 'Gravity in 30 seconds', with five captions. On the Earth a 1 kg mass weighs 10 N; on the Moon 1.6 N; on Mars 3.8 N; on Jupiter 25.4 N; take the weight to be in proportion to the mass. For each caption, say whether it is correct; if it is wrong, write the corrected caption.
1. 'The Earth pulls only things that are falling; a book lying on a table is not pulled at all.'
2. 'At the top of its path, a ball thrown straight up is at rest for a moment, so no force acts on it there.'
3. 'On Mars, a 1 kg packet has a mass of only 0.38 kg.'
4. 'A coin that weighs 0.1 N on the Earth would weigh 0.016 N on the Moon.'
5. 'A 4 kg school bag weighs 40 N on the Earth and 101.6 N on Jupiter.'
questions.a: 1. Wrong: the Earth attracts all objects towards itself; the resting book is pulled too (that pull is its weight). 2. Wrong: the Earth's gravitational force still pulls the ball down at the top; that is why its direction of motion changes and it starts to fall. 3. Wrong: its mass is still 1 kg on Mars; it is its weight that changes, to 3.8 N. 4. Correct: the coin's mass is 0.1 / 10 = 0.01 kg, and 0.01 x 1.6 = 0.016 N. 5. Correct: 4 x 10 = 40 N and 4 x 25.4 = 101.6 N.
s: Caption 1 wrong, corrected: the Earth pulls all objects
Caption 2 wrong: gravity still acts at the top and reverses the motion
Caption 3 wrong: mass stays 1 kg, weight is 3.8 N
Caption 4 correct, checked: 0.01 kg x 1.6 = 0.016 N
Caption 5 correct, checked: 40 N and 101.6 N

questions.q:
Jaya hangs a large, empty cardboard carton and then a small iron weight, one at a time, from the same spring balance. Each pulls the pointer to 3 N.
(a) Does the Earth pull one of them more strongly than the other? Explain from the readings.
(b) Her brother says, 'The carton must be heavier because it is so much bigger.' Correct him using what weight means.
questions.a: (a) No. A spring balance measures weight, the force with which the Earth pulls an object; both stretch the spring to 3 N, so the Earth pulls them equally hard. (b) Weight measures how strongly the Earth pulls an object, which the balance shows by the stretch of the spring, not by how big the object looks. The big carton and the small iron weight both weigh 3 N.
s: Equal pull, because both readings are 3 N of weight
Weight is the strength of the Earth's pull shown by the stretch, not the size of the object

questions.q:
A student's record reads:
'Mass of stone on the Earth: 2 kg. Mass of the same stone on Mars: 0.76 kg. Weight of the stone on Mars: 7.6 N.'
On Mars a 1 kg mass weighs 3.8 N; take the weight to be in proportion to the mass. Show that the record cannot be fully correct, find the wrong entry, and correct it.
questions.a: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and remains the same at every place, so the stone cannot have a mass of 2 kg on the Earth and 0.76 kg on Mars. The wrong entry is the mass on Mars; it should be 2 kg. The weight entry is right: 2 x 3.8 = 7.6 N.
s: States that mass cannot change from place to place
Identifies the Mars mass entry as wrong and corrects it to 2 kg
Checks the weight entry: 2 x 3.8 = 7.6 N is correct

questions.q: A 3 kg object hung from a spring balance on some planet reads 27 N. A 1 kg mass weighs 10 N on the Earth, 3.8 N on Mars, 9 N on Venus and 25.4 N on Jupiter. Taking the weight to be in proportion to the mass, where is the object?
questions.a: Venus 27 / 3 = 9 N for each kilogram, which matches Venus.
o: Venus
Earth
Jupiter
Mars

questions.q:
Sumit was told to read only the newton scale of a spring balance with a range of 0 to 10 N and 5 equal small divisions between each pair of 1 N marks. He copied his readings into a table whose only column is headed 'Weight (N)':
Row 1: Pencil box: 2.4 N
Row 2: Partly filled water bottle: 6.7 N
Row 3: Geometry box: 0.3 kg
Row 4: Full water jug: 14 N
(a) Explain why the entry in Row 2 cannot be a reading of this scale.
(b) What is wrong with Row 3 as an entry in this table?
(c) What is wrong with Row 4, and what should Sumit have done instead?
(d) Which one row can go into the final table unchanged? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) One small division is 1 N / 5 = 0.2 N, so readings go up in steps of 0.2 N (6.6 N, 6.8 N); 6.7 N lies between two marks and cannot be read on this scale. (b) The column is for weight read on the newton scale, but 0.3 kg is a mass: the kilogram is a unit of mass, and weight is a force that must be written in newton. (c) 14 N is more than the 10 N the balance can measure: the jug should not have been hung, as it may damage the balance; he should use a balance with a larger range. (d) Row 1: 2.4 N is a whole number of 0.2 N steps (12 divisions), it is within the 10 N range, and it is in newton.
s: Row 2: 6.7 N is not a multiple of the 0.2 N division
Row 3: 0.3 kg is a mass in a weight column; weight needs newton
Row 4: exceeds the 10 N range, may damage it; use a larger-range balance
Keeps Row 1, checking steps, range and unit

questions.q:
Diya pushes a tightly closed, empty plastic bottle down into a bucket of water and lets go. (Use: if the buoyant force on an object under water is greater than the gravitational force on it, the object is pushed up.) Explain each observation in terms of the forces acting on the bottle.
(i) While pushing the bottle down, she feels her hand being pushed up.
(ii) When she lets go, the bottle shoots up to the surface.
(iii) It then floats at the surface with part of it above the water.
questions.a: (i) The water applies an upward force, the buoyant force (upthrust), on the bottle, which pushes back against her hand. (ii) Fully under water, the buoyant force on the light bottle is greater than the Earth's gravitational force on it, so it is pushed up. (iii) At the surface, the bottle floats because the gravitational force on it and the buoyant force on it are equal.
s: (i) Upward buoyant force of the water
(ii) Buoyant force greater than gravitational force when fully under
(iii) Floating: gravitational and buoyant forces equal

questions.q: Kunal holds a rubber ball fully under the water of a swimming pool and then lets go. Which forces act on the ball just after he lets go?
questions.a: The Earth's pull downward and the water's push upward The Earth's gravitational force acts on all objects, in water too, and the water applies an upward buoyant force on any object placed in it; his hand no longer touches the ball.
o: The Earth's pull downward and the water's push upward
Only the water's upward push, as gravity stops in water
Only the Earth's pull, as water pushes only floating things
His hand's push and the water's push, both upward

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'A plastic duck floating in a bathtub has no gravitational force acting on it; that is why it does not sink.'
questions.a: False. The Earth's gravitational force still pulls the duck downward; the duck floats because the water's upward buoyant force on it is equal to this gravitational force.
s: States False
Explains that gravity still acts and floating means the buoyant force equals it

questions.q:
A science club in Bhubaneswar holds four objects fully under water, one at a time, and finds the weight of water each pushes aside (displaces).
Object P, a cork ball: weight 0.4 N; water displaced when fully under: 2.0 N
Object Q, an iron bolt: weight 3.9 N; water displaced when fully under: 0.5 N
Object R, a sealed bottle partly filled with sand: weight 5.0 N; water displaced when fully under: 5.0 N
Object S, a lump of clay: weight 6.0 N; water displaced when fully under: 3.0 N
(a) What is the buoyant force on Q while it is fully under water?
(b) Which objects sink? Explain using Archimedes' Principle.
(c) P ends up floating at the surface. What weight of water does it displace there?
(d) A student ties the cork ball P to the iron bolt Q and says the cork will keep the bolt afloat. Treat the pair as one object, fully under water. Decide whether it floats or sinks.
questions.a: (a) 0.5 N: by Archimedes' Principle, the upward force equals the weight of the liquid displaced. (b) Q and S: the weight of water each displaces (0.5 N and 3.0 N) is smaller than its weight (3.9 N and 6.0 N), so each sinks. (c) 0.4 N: a floating object has a buoyant force equal to its weight, and the buoyant force equals the weight of water displaced. (d) It sinks: the pair weighs 0.4 + 3.9 = 4.3 N but, even fully under, displaces only 2.0 + 0.5 = 2.5 N of water, which is less than 4.3 N.
s: Buoyant force on Q is 0.5 N
Q and S sink because displaced water weighs less than the object
Floating P displaces 0.4 N of water
Pair: 4.3 N against at most 2.5 N, so it sinks

questions.q: A coconut that weighs 15 N floats in a village pond, partly above the water. What is the weight of the water it displaces?
questions.a: 15 N A floating object displaces liquid whose weight equals its own weight (Archimedes' Principle), so 15 N.
o: 0 N, because a floating object displaces no water
More than 15 N, or else it would sink
Less than 15 N, as part of it is above the water

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A lump of pumice rock can float on water.
Reason (R): Pumice forms when lava full of gas cools quickly and traps tiny bubbles, giving a light, porous rock filled with air pockets.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The trapped air pockets make the rock light enough that the water's buoyant force can balance its weight, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Sneha places a sealed plastic ball in a bowl of water, where it floats. She then lowers a steel ball into a bowl of cooking oil, where it sinks to the bottom.
(a) Does the oil apply any upward force on the steel ball, even though the ball sinks? Name the force.
(b) For each ball, compare the Earth's pull on it with the upward force of the liquid.
questions.a: (a) Yes. All liquids, not only water, apply an upward force on an object placed in them; this is the buoyant force (upthrust), and it acts on the steel ball even though the ball sinks. (b) Plastic ball in water: the gravitational force and the buoyant force are equal, so it floats. Steel ball in oil: the gravitational force is more than the buoyant force, so it sinks.
s: Yes: every liquid applies an upward buoyant force, also on an object that sinks
Floating plastic ball: forces equal; sinking steel ball: gravitational force greater

questions.q:
Match each object in Column I with the buoyant force acting on it in Column II.
Column I
1. A raft weighing 900 N floating on a lake
2. A stone weighing 900 N lying on a pond bed, displacing 300 N of water
3. A sealed drum weighing 900 N held fully under water, displacing 1500 N of water
4. A stone weighing 900 N resting on a dry jetty
Column II
(a) 900 N
(b) 300 N
(c) 1500 N
(d) 0 N
questions.a: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d. A floating raft has a buoyant force equal to its weight; a fully immersed object has a buoyant force equal to the weight of liquid it displaces (300 N and 1500 N); a liquid applies buoyant force only on objects placed in it, so the stone on the dry jetty has none.

questions.q:
A flood-rescue team in Assam builds a raft from sealed empty plastic drums tied under a wooden platform; the platform always stays above the water. Each drum weighs 20 N and, when pushed fully under water, displaces water weighing 600 N. The platform weighs 400 N. A family of five must cross: four adults who weigh 550 N each and a child who weighs 400 N (take these weights as exact).
(a) With 4 drums, what is the largest upward force the water can apply on the drums? (1)
(b) What is the buoyant force on the empty 4-drum raft as it floats? Give the reason. (1)
(c) Show that the 4-drum raft can carry three adults but not three adults and the child. (1)
(d) The team adds a fifth drum. Show what happens to the 5-drum raft if the whole family boards at once. (1)
(e) Should the family cross in one trip on the 5-drum raft or in two trips? Decide, using (d), and suggest groups for the trips. (1)
questions.a: (a) By Archimedes' Principle the upward force equals the weight of water displaced: 4 x 600 = 2400 N, when all four drums are fully under. (b) The empty raft weighs 4 x 20 + 400 = 480 N; a floating object has a buoyant force equal to its weight, so 480 N. (c) Three adults: 480 + 3 x 550 = 2130 N, less than 2400 N, so it floats. Adding the child: 2130 + 400 = 2530 N, more than 2400 N, so it would sink. (d) The 5-drum raft weighs 5 x 20 + 400 = 500 N; with the whole family the total is 500 + 4 x 550 + 400 = 3100 N, more than the largest buoyant force of 5 x 600 = 3000 N, so the raft would sink. (e) Two trips. One trip needs 3100 N of buoyant force but the drums can give at most 3000 N. For example two adults and the child (500 + 1100 + 400 = 2000 N), then the other two adults (500 + 1100 = 1600 N); each is less than 3000 N.
s: Largest upward force 2400 N, from the weight of water displaced
Empty raft floats with buoyant force 480 N, equal to its weight
2130 N fits within 2400 N; 2530 N exceeds it
5-drum raft with family: 3100 N exceeds 3000 N, so it sinks
Chooses two trips because the total exceeds the largest buoyant force, with valid groups

questions.q: A stone weighing 9 N is lowered completely into a tank and pushes aside water weighing 3.5 N. The buoyant force acting on the stone is ___ N.

Here are two facts about an object: its weight is 12 N, and when it is held fully under water it displaces water weighing 20 N. Write a short real-life situation with an object that fits these facts. Then say (i) what happens when it is released under water, and (ii) the weight of water it displaces once it is floating.
questions.a: Sample: a sealed plastic jerrycan with a little water in it, weighing 12 N, is pushed fully under a pond by a child and displaces 20 N of water. (i) When released, it is pushed up, because the buoyant force (20 N) is greater than its weight (12 N), and it rises to the surface. (ii) Floating, it displaces water weighing 12 N, equal to its weight.
s: A realistic object fitting a 12 N weight and 20 N displacement
Rises when released, since 20 N is more than 12 N
Floating, it displaces 12 N of water

questions.q:
A fishing boat weighing 8000 N floats on Chilika lake. The fishermen load 1500 N of fish into it, and it still floats, but sits lower in the water.
(a) What is the buoyant force on the boat before and after loading?
(b) Using Archimedes' Principle, explain why the loaded boat sits lower in the water.
questions.a: (a) Before: 8000 N; after: 8000 + 1500 = 9500 N, because a floating object has a buoyant force equal to its (total) weight. (b) The buoyant force equals the weight of water displaced, so the loaded boat must displace water weighing 9500 N instead of 8000 N; it can push aside more water only by sinking further into it, so more of the hull is under water.
s: 8000 N before and 9500 N after, equal to the weight each time
More water (9500 N) must be displaced, so more of the hull goes under

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: All liquids, not only water, apply an upward force on objects placed in them.
Statement 2: When an object floats, the weight of the liquid it displaces is equal to its own weight.
Statement 3: An object sinks if the buoyant force on it is greater than the gravitational force on it.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only. Statement 3 is reversed: an object sinks when the gravitational force on it is more than the buoyant force.
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 2 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Anika wrote up a test.
Step 1: A stone hung from a spring balance in air reads 5.0 N.
Step 2: The same stone, hung from the balance fully under water, reads 3.2 N.
Step 3: The water that overflowed from a brim-full can when the stone went in weighs 1.8 N.
Conclusion 1: 'The stone lost 1.8 N because the water took away part of its mass.'
Conclusion 2: 'The balance still shows 3.2 N, so the stone will float if it is released.'
(a) What does the fall in the reading from Step 1 to Step 2 measure, and how do Steps 1 to 3 support your answer?
(b) Correct Conclusion 1.
(c) Correct Conclusion 2.
(d) The same stone is then hung fully inside a liquid in which it displaces liquid weighing 2.3 N. Predict the balance reading.
questions.a: (a) The buoyant force on the stone. The liquid pushes up on the stone, so the balance has to hold up less: the fall is 5.0 - 3.2 = 1.8 N, and by Archimedes' Principle the upward force equals the weight of water displaced, which Step 3 measures as 1.8 N, so the two agree. (b) The stone's mass does not change; the water pushes up on it with a buoyant force of 1.8 N, so the balance reads less. (c) The stone will sink: the weight of the water it displaces (1.8 N) is less than its weight (5.0 N); the gravitational force is greater than the buoyant force. (d) The buoyant force is now 2.3 N (the weight of liquid displaced), so the reading is 5.0 - 2.3 = 2.7 N.
s: The 1.8 N fall is the buoyant force, matching the 1.8 N overflow
Mass unchanged; the drop is due to the water's upward push
The stone sinks because 1.8 N is less than 5.0 N
Predicts 5.0 - 2.3 = 2.7 N

questions.q: A riddle page in a children's magazine says: 'Big, heavy things always sink in water and small, light things always float.' A log weighing 2000 N floats down the Brahmaputra while a steel pin weighing 0.05 N sinks in a glass of water. Is the magazine right, wrong or partly right? Explain the two observations using what decides floating and sinking.
questions.a: Wrong. Floating or sinking does not depend on how heavy an object is by itself but on how its weight compares with the buoyant force (the weight of liquid it displaces). The log floats because the water it displaces weighs as much as the log, 2000 N, so the buoyant force equals its weight. The pin sinks because, even fully under water, the water it displaces weighs less than 0.05 N, so the gravitational force on it is greater than the buoyant force.
s: Verdict: wrong
Explains the floating log: displaced water's weight equals its 2000 N weight
Explains the sinking pin: displaced water weighs less than the pin

questions.q:
Four toys are each held fully under water and their weights compared with the weight of water each displaces.
Toy A: weight 1.2 N, displaces 1.5 N
Toy B: weight 2.0 N, displaces 1.6 N
Toy C: weight 0.9 N, displaces 0.9 N
Toy D: weight 3.1 N, displaces 2.8 N
Which toys will sink when released?
questions.a: B and D only. An object sinks when the weight of liquid it displaces is smaller than its own weight: B (1.6 N < 2.0 N) and D (2.8 N < 3.1 N). A displaces more than its weight and rises; C displaces exactly its weight and floats.
o: B and D only
B only
B, C and D
A and C only

questions.q:
A sealed bottle weighs 3 N. Lalitha pushes it slowly down into a bucket of water and notes the weight of water it displaces: one-third under, 2 N; half under, 3 N; fully under, 6 N.
(a) At which of these three positions would the bottle stay floating if she let go? Why?
(b) She lets go when it is fully under. What happens, and how much of the bottle is under water when it settles?
questions.a: (a) Half under: there it displaces 3 N of water, so the buoyant force (3 N) equals its weight (3 N), and an object floats when the two are equal. (b) It is pushed up, because the buoyant force (6 N) is more than its weight (3 N); it rises and settles floating with half of it under water, where the displaced water weighs 3 N, equal to its weight.
s: Half under, where buoyant force 3 N equals the weight
Rises from fully under (6 N > 3 N) and settles half under

questions.q:
The chapter gives two ways to decide whether an object floats or sinks in a liquid.
Way 1: compare the gravitational force on the object with the buoyant force on it.
Way 2 (Archimedes' Principle): compare the weight of the liquid the object displaces with the weight of the object.
(a) Explain why Way 1 and Way 2 always give the same answer. (2)
(b) An object weighs 7 N and, fully under water, displaces water weighing 5 N. Apply each way separately to decide what happens. (2)
(c) Another object also weighs 7 N but floats. State the buoyant force on it and the weight of the water it displaces. (1)
questions.a: (a) The gravitational force on an object is its weight, and by Archimedes' Principle the buoyant force equals the weight of the liquid displaced. So 'gravitational force versus buoyant force' and 'object's weight versus weight of liquid displaced' compare exactly the same two quantities. (b) Way 1: gravitational force 7 N is more than the buoyant force 5 N, so it sinks. Way 2: the displaced water (5 N) weighs less than the object (7 N), so it sinks. (c) Buoyant force 7 N; displaced water weighs 7 N.
s: Weight is the gravitational force
Buoyant force equals the weight of liquid displaced, so both ways compare the same quantities
Way 1: 7 N more than 5 N, sinks
Way 2: 5 N less than 7 N, sinks
Floating 7 N object: buoyant force 7 N and 7 N of water displaced

questions.q:
Two identical plastic bottles are tightly closed: one is empty, the other is filled to the brim with sand. Each is held fully under water and released. The empty one shoots up; the sand-filled one sinks.
(a) Is the buoyant force on the two bottles the same or different while both are fully under water? Why?
(b) Why, then, does one rise and the other sink?
questions.a: (a) The same: identical bottles fully under water push aside the same amount of water, and the buoyant force equals the weight of the water displaced. (b) The sand-filled bottle is much heavier: its weight (gravitational force) is more than this buoyant force, so it sinks, while the empty bottle's weight is less than the buoyant force, so it is pushed up.
s: Same buoyant force because the same water is displaced
The weights differ: more than the buoyant force for the sand bottle, less for the empty one

questions.q: Raju draws a full bucket of water up from a well with a rope. At which position does the bucket feel lightest to pull?
questions.a: While it is still fully under the water. Under the water the water's buoyant force pushes up on the bucket; once part of it is out, it displaces less water and the upward push is smaller, and out of the water there is none. Once the bucket clears the surface, the rope must also hold up the water inside it, so it feels heaviest then.
o: While it is still fully under the water
When it is half out of the water
When it has just come fully out of the water
The same everywhere, as its mass does not change

questions.q: A sealed tin weighing 1.5 N floats in a pond. A frog weighing 0.4 N jumps onto it, and the tin still floats. Write the number only: the weight of water the tin now displaces is ___ N.
